scenes.spec: car rolling to a stop at an intersection, exterior close on front wheel
scenes.narration: There are car noises you can think about for a week. There are noises you should handle this month. And then there's this one — the low, granular grinding when you press the brake pedal, like stepping on gravel that someone installed inside your wheel. Grinding is the one brake noise that is almost never innocent, because of what's physically making it: in most cases, by the time you hear a grind, something that was supposed to be there... isn't anymore. Ten minutes, and you'll know exactly what wore away, what it's costing you per mile, and the one version of this noise that's actually harmless.

scenes.spec: channel card — "Why Is My Car Doing That?"
three-way split — "Grinds ONLY while braking" / "Grinds while rolling, brake or not" / "Grinds on the first stops of the day"
scenes.narration: Pin down when the grind happens, because the three patterns have three different bank accounts attached. **Only while braking** — pedal down, grind starts; pedal up, grind stops. That's the classic, and the most urgent. It usually means friction material is *gone*. **While rolling, whether or not you brake** — a rhythmic grind or growl tied to wheel speed, maybe changing when you swerve gently. That's usually not brakes at all — that's a wheel bearing, and it gets its own episode. We'll cover the quick tell later. **First stops of the morning only** — a soft grind or scrape for the first half-mile that fades. Same overnight surface rust from our squeak episode, being scrubbed off the rotors. This is the harmless one.

scenes.section: THE MECHANISM — WHAT A GRIND PHYSICALLY IS
scenes.spec: pad side-view from ep 2 — friction material worn to nothing, steel backing plate contacting the rotor face
scenes.narration: A brake pad is a steel **backing plate** carrying a thick block of **friction material**. That material is the part designed to touch the rotor. It wears down over tens of thousands of miles — through the squealing wear-indicator stage we covered last episode — and if the squeal gets ignored long enough, the friction material wears through completely. Now the steel backing plate presses directly against the steel rotor.

scenes.section: THE MECHANISM — WHAT A GRIND PHYSICALLY IS
scenes.spec: rotor strip from ep 1 — backing plate gouging the surface, sparks of material, grooves deepening pass after pass
scenes.narration: Steel grinding steel is exactly what it sounds like. And it cuts both ways: every stop machines grooves into the rotor face, turning a smooth disc into a vinyl record. Braking performance drops — steel-on-steel has a fraction of the friction your pads had [TECH CONFIRM — comfortable stating "stopping distances grow noticeably," or want a stronger/softer phrasing?] — and the rotor, which might have survived one more pad change, becomes scrap metal cutting itself deeper every mile. That's why grinding is the expensive noise: **the longer it runs, the bigger the parts list.**

scenes.section: CAUSE #1 — PADS WORN TO THE BACKING PLATE (the usual suspect)
scenes.spec: pad wear timeline — new pad, worn pad with squealer touching, pad gone with plate contact, each stage dated
scenes.narration: The wear-out story has a schedule. New pads. Tens of thousands of miles of quiet service. Then the wear-indicator squeal — the built-in appointment reminder — for a while [TECH CONFIRM — restate your squeal-to-grind runway estimate from ep 2 so the numbers agree]. Then the squeal *changes character*: lower, rougher, granular. That change is the moment friction material ran out. One detail worth knowing: pads on the same axle rarely wear identically. A grinding *left* front with a surviving *right* front is common — which is why the fix is always per-axle, never per-wheel.

scenes.section: CAUSE #2 — A STONE OR DEBRIS BETWEEN PAD AND ROTOR
scenes.spec: caliper area with a small stone lodged between rotor and splash shield, scraping ring drawn on rotor
scenes.narration: Sometimes the grind arrives *suddenly*, on a car with healthy pads — often right after gravel, a dirt road, or roadwork. A pebble kicked up into the caliper area can lodge between the rotor and the **splash shield** (the thin metal plate behind the disc), scraping a bright ring into the rotor with a sound completely out of proportion to its size. The tell: it appears out of nowhere, sometimes grinds even *without* braking, and can vanish as suddenly as it came if the stone dislodges. Caught early it's the cheapest fix in this episode — sometimes zero parts, just removal. [TECH CONFIRM — how often do you see debris grinds vs worn-pad grinds? And is bending the splash shield back the usual resolution?]

scenes.spec: rotor face with deep grooves and rust pitting, pad riding the ridges
scenes.narration: A car that sat for weeks — airport lot, storage, a long trip — grows more than surface rust. Deep pitting takes hold, and the first hundred miles of driving can sound genuinely alarming as pads try to re-seat against a cratered surface. Mild cases scrub clean and go quiet. Deep pitting doesn't: the pad rides the high spots, the grind persists, and the rotor needs machining or replacement. [TECH CONFIRM — your rule of thumb for "sat too long, rotors won't recover" — weeks? months? climate-dependent?]

scenes.section: CAUSE #4 — IT'S NOT THE BRAKES: THE WHEEL BEARING FAKE-OUT
scenes.spec: hub assembly from ep 1 — bearing races highlighted, grinding waves drawn from hub, not pad contact
scenes.narration: The impostor. A failing wheel bearing grinds, growls, or hums — but tied to **wheel speed, not brake pedal**. Quick roadside test, safe version: find an empty stretch, gentle S-weave at low speed. Bearing noise typically *changes* as weight shifts onto and off the bad wheel — often quieter turning one way, louder the other. Brake-pad grinding doesn't care about the weave; it cares about the pedal. [TECH CONFIRM — bless the S-weave description as the safe DIY tell, or give me your preferred version] If your grind fails the pedal test and passes the weave test — stop guessing, that's a bearing, and a failing bearing is a today-not-next-week problem. Full episode on it later in the season.

scenes.spec: three-tier verdict card — "Scrub it off" / "Days, not weeks" / "Park it"
scenes.narration: **Scrub it off:** morning-only surface-rust grind that fades within a mile. Fine. Monitor that it *always* fades. **Days, not weeks:** any grind that happens every time you brake. You're machining your own rotors at every stop light. It will not improve on its own, and the parts list grows with the odometer. **Park it:** grinding *plus* a soft or sinking pedal, grinding *plus* the car pulling hard under braking, or bearing-grind that's gotten loud. Those combinations mean the system's ability to stop the car is actively degrading. Tow money is cheaper than crash money. [TECH CONFIRM — bless the tiers, especially "park it" criteria]

So: a grind that lives on the brake pedal is metal that ran out of material — pads done, rotors on the clock. A sudden grind on healthy brakes is probably a stone in the works. A grind that rolls with the wheels and shifts when you weave is a bearing wearing a brake costume. And the only free grind is the morning rust-scrub that fades in a mile. Your brakes gave you two warnings before this — the squeal, then the grind. Next episode, we go back to the beginning of that story: the shake in the steering wheel that starts it all.
